CausalChain: Chronic liver fibrosis → Increased matrix stiffness → Activation of integrin β5/FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in TAMs → Upregulation of HIF‐1α and LOXL2 → Metabolic reprogramming toward fatty acid oxidation and enhanced glycolysis → Increased PD‐L1 expression on TAMs → Suppression of CD8+ T cell cytotoxicity → Tumor progression
Hypothesis: Increased extracellular matrix stiffness in the fibrotic liver drives immunosuppressive TAM polarization through integrin‐mediated FAK/MEK/ERK signaling, leading to metabolic reprogramming and upregulation of PD‐L1. Inhibiting this mechanotransduction pathway in TAMs will reprogram their metabolism, reduce PD‐L1 expression, restore CD8+ T cell function, and enhance the efficacy of immunotherapies in liver cancer.
Abstract: Liver cancer is frequently accompanied by chronic fibrosis and increased matrix stiffness, conditions that profoundly influence the tumor immune microenvironment. Recent studies have linked the mechanical properties of the liver, such as increased stiffness, with altered macrophage phenotypes via integrin‐mediated signaling pathways. In this context, we propose that the elevated extracellular matrix rigidity activates integrin‐driven FAK/MEK/ERK signaling in tumor‐associated macrophages (TAMs), which leads to metabolic reprogramming favoring fatty acid oxidation and glycolytic regulation of PD‐L1. This metabolic shift increases immunosuppressive functions of TAMs, reduces CD8+ T cell infiltration, and ultimately promotes tumor progression. Here, we outline a mechanistic rationale for targeting the mechanotransduction axis in TAMs as a novel approach to reprogram these cells toward an M1 phenotype, thereby enhancing the response to immune checkpoint inhibitors in liver cancer.
